finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id performs no authorization. authorize() is called without await, so its 403 rejection is dropped and the report is deleted anyway.
finding.source: Path parameter req.params.id (server.js:19), reachable by any request to the route. Caller identity comes from req.user, set from req.session.user (server.js:5).
finding.sink: db.reports.remove(report.id) at server.js:21, a destructive write.

trace.note: authorize(req.user,'delete',report) called without await; the returned promise is dropped.
Inside authorize: grants lookup. Lines 11-14 throw a 403 when 'delete' is not granted, which rejects a promise nobody awaits.
Deletion runs regardless of the authorization outcome.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() exists and throws on missing grant (server.js:9-16). The PUT handler at server.js:27 awaits the same call, so the DELETE omission departs from the local pattern. No try/catch and no route-level auth middleware in this file. If req.user is undefined, line 10 throws a TypeError that is also dropped, so deletion still proceeds. Whether unauthenticated requests are blocked upstream depends on session middleware not present in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none. authorize() (server.js:9-16) throws a 403 at server.js:14, but the call at server.js:20 is a bare statement with no await and no try/catch, so the rejection is discarded and the remove at server.js:21 runs. The PUT handler at server.js:27 awaits the same call, so the DELETE omission is the only difference. The directory contains only server.js, so no session or route middleware exists here to block the request.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: the handler at server.js:18-23 calls authorize() without await at line 20, so the 403 from server.js:14 is dropped and db.reports.remove runs at line 21 for any caller, including an authenticated user who lacks the delete grant. The attacker only needs a session, not admin rights, and nothing in the file blocks the call. The only uncertainty is upstream session middleware outside this directory, which could restrict who reaches the route but would not restore the check.

finding.claim: Dropped authorize() rejections become unhandled promise rejections that can crash the Node process. A nonexistent id triggers the same path.
finding.source: Path parameter req.params.id (server.js:19), reachable by any request.
finding.sink: Process availability. Node 15+ default unhandled-rejection mode terminates the process.

trace.note: db.reports.get returns null for an unknown id.
authorize receives null; line 10 reads resource.id and throws a TypeError, which is dropped because the call is not awaited.
report.id throws a TypeError inside the async handler, rejecting it.
PUT variant: await authorize with null resource throws at line 10; Express 4 does not catch async rejections, so the request hangs and the rejection is unhandled.

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch or error-handling middleware in this file. Impact depends on Express major version and on any process-level unhandledRejection handler, neither of which is visible in this repo.

verdict.guard_found: None in server.js. There is no try/catch or error middleware (server.js:18-30), and the `authorize` call at server.js:20 is a bare, unawaited statement, so its rejection is discarded. The only guard is the `grants.includes` check at server.js:11, which throws and is never reached with a null resource. Session middleware (server.js:5) and any unhandledRejection handler or Express version are not in the repo.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: for an unknown id, db.reports.get returns null (server.js:19), authorize's rejection on resource.id (server.js:10) is never awaited or caught (server.js:20), and report.id at server.js:21 throws inside the async handler, so unhandled rejections occur with nothing in server.js to stop them. The crash outcome additionally depends on Node 15+ defaults and the absence of a process-level handler, which the repo cannot show. Separately, the same unawaited call at server.js:20 means a DELETE on an existing report where the caller lacks "delete" grants proceeds to db.reports.remove at server.js:21, because the 403 is thrown into the void. That is a larger authorization bypass than the candidate reports and should be filed separately.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id mass assignment: the entire client JSON body is written to the stored record without field filtering.
finding.source: req.body (server.js:28), parsed unconditionally by express.json() at server.js:3, supplied by any caller with write access to the report.
finding.sink: db.reports.update(report.id, req.body) at server.js:28, a persistent write to report storage.

trace.note: await authorize(..., 'write', report) enforces the write grant against the stored record.
Entire req.body passed to update; no allow-list of writable fields.

finding.guards_checked: Write grant is awaited and checked against the target record. report.id comes from the database, not the body. No field allow-list in this file. Whether schema fields such as owner, grants, or id are writable cannot be confirmed without the db layer. Confidence is low to medium.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)`, which throws a 403 when the write grant is missing (server.js:11-14), so the call is awaited and its failure aborts the handler before the write. No field allow-list exists anywhere in server.js, and nothing in the file restricts which body keys reach db.reports.update at server.js:28.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (server.js:25-28), and the write grant is enforced at server.js:27, but whether the unfiltered body at server.js:28 lets a write-grant holder change security-relevant fields such as owner, grants, or id depends on the db.reports.update implementation and schema, which are not in the directory, so the impact cannot be decided from the code available.
